title: Sampling Bias Simulator
summary: A generated population of 4,000 fictional students whose true average weekly study hours is printed on screen. Learners recruit from it by convenience, self-selection, year quotas, stratified random sampling or simple random sampling, set how much more likely commuters and students with jobs are to decline, and watch repeated estimates land on a number line beside the truth. Raising the sample size tightens the cloud of estimates without moving it, which is the whole distinction between variability and bias.
learningObjectives: Separate sampling variability from systematic selection bias using repeated draws from a known population.
Explain why increasing the sample size narrows the interval and cannot move a biased estimate.
Describe what a quota corrects and what it leaves untouched.
State the condition a probability sample still needs in order to remain unbiased.
Identify which practical changes to a survey reduce bias rather than scatter.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the population is generated and every sample drawn in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native radios, ranges, a number input and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the two sliders announce meaningful values such as '90 per cent tilt: commuters and students with jobs are that much more likely to decline'. The estimate line is hidden from assistive technology and every figure it carries is repeated in a definition list beneath it - population mean, current estimate, difference from truth, and the running average of all draws - plus a full table of every draw behind a disclosure control. On the line itself the truth is a solid rule with its own printed value, previous estimates are hollow circles and the current estimate is a filled diamond with an interval bar, so shape rather than colour carries the distinction. The composition table names each group and prints both population and sample percentages. Every draw announces a full sentence through the polite live region. Focus moves to the simulator heading when it unlocks, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Sampling bias against sampling variability: why a bigger sample cannot fix the wrong people
simulationNotes: A population of 4,000 fictional students generated once from a fixed seed of 20260807, so its true mean of 11.29 weekly study hours is identical in every browser. Each student has a year of study, a commuting status and a part-time job, and hours are 12.6 plus year effects, minus 2.2 for commuting and 3.0 for a job, plus normal noise with a standard deviation of 4, floored at zero; the population mean is computed from the generated population rather than asserted. Recruitment is weighted sampling without replacement by the exponential-race method, which reduces exactly to simple random sampling when all weights are equal. Convenience and quota weights penalise commuters and job-holders and rise with the person's own study hours, which is selection on the outcome itself; volunteer weights favour first years and heavier studiers; stratified and simple random sampling use equal weights. The non-response dial multiplies every weight by a response probability that falls with commuting and holding a job, and applies to the probability methods too, so a random sample becomes biased once non-response is differential. Response probability enters the weight rather than reducing the achieved sample, which is the equivalent of recruiting until the target is met. The selection weights are invented to make the effect legible and are not measured quantities; real non-response depends on topic, mode, incentive and season and is not one dial. No real institution, register, survey or student is described.
